rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: One parsing makes alif-lām-mīm the first subject, “that” a second subject, and “the Book” its predicate; this presents the Qur’an as the complete Book, with other books deficient by comparison.
rows.anchor: أن يكون { الم } مبتدأ و { ذالك } مبتدأ ثانيا و { الكتاب } خبره والجملة خبر المبتدأ الأول

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Alternatively, “the Book” is an adjective, and “that Book” means the promised Book.
rows.anchor: وأن يكون الكتاب صفة ، ومعناه هو ذلك الكتاب الموعود

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Alif-lām-mīm may predicate an omitted subject (“these letters”), followed by “that Book” as a second predicate or apposition, with “the Book” adjectival.
rows.anchor: وأن يكون { الم } خبر مبتدأ محذوف أي هذه { الم * ويكون * ذالك الكتاب } خبرا ثانيا أو بدلا على أن الكتاب صفة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another analysis treats alif-lām-mīm and “that Book” as two separate sentences.
rows.anchor: وأن تكون هذه { الم } جملة و { ذالك الكتاب } جملة أخرى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: If alif-lām-mīm is treated as a sound, “that” may be subject with “the Book” its predicate, or “the Book” an adjective, or an omitted subject may mean “composed of these letters.”
rows.anchor: وإن جعلت { الم } بمنزلة الصوت كان { ذالك } مبتدأ وخبره { الكتاب } أي ذلك الكتاب المنزل هو الكتاب الكامل

rows.speaker: عبد الله
rows.claim: Abdullah’s reading connects these letters directly to “the sending down of the Book”; al-Rāzī says this composition is evident.
rows.anchor: وقرأ عبد الله { الم * تنزيل الكتاب لا ريب فيه } ( السجدة : 2 ) وتأليف هذا ظاهر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Rayb is close to doubt but adds suspicion of something bad; “rābanī” means that I suspected something bad of someone.
rows.anchor: الريب قريب من الشك ، . وفيه زيادة ، كأنه ظن سوء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Rayb can also mean the events of time or what stirs anger in the heart; both usages return to doubt, since feared events are possible and inward agitation is uncertain. The verse and poem illustrate these usages.
rows.anchor: هذان قد يرجعان إلى معنى الشك ، لأن ما يخاف من ريب المنون محتمل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verse denies that the Book gives any ground for doubt: its truth, divine origin, and miraculous character are beyond reasonable suspicion.
rows.anchor: والمقصود أنه لا شبهة في صحته ، ولا في كونه من عند الله

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Reading the denial specifically as denying doubt in the Qur’an’s miraculousness is especially apt because 2:23 challenges doubters to match what was sent down.
rows.anchor: على الخصوص كان أقرب لتأكيد هذا التأويل بقوله : { وإن كنتم فى ريب مما نزلنا على عبدنا }

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Against the objection that people do in fact doubt the Qur’an, or that God’s own lack of doubt would be pointless, al-Rāzī says its clarity is such that no reasonable person ought to doubt it; Arab eloquence could not match even its shortest sūra.
rows.anchor: بلغ في الوضوح إلى حيث لا ينبغي لمرتاب أن يرتاب فيه ، والأمر كذلك

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The order puts the most important denial first: “no doubt in it” avoids suggesting that some other book is doubtful while this one is not.
rows.anchor: يقدمون الأهم فالأهم ، وههنا الأهم نفي الريب بالكلية عن الكتاب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The contrast with “no harm in it” in 37:47 serves a different purpose: it distinguishes the wine of Paradise, which does not impair reason, from worldly wine.
rows.anchor: كما قصد في قوله : { لا فيها غول } تفضيل خمر الجنة على خمور الدنيا

rows.speaker: أبو الشعثاء
rows.claim: Abū al-Shaʿthāʾ reads “lā rayba fīhi” with rayb in the nominative.
rows.anchor: قرأ أبو الشعثاء { لا ريب فيه } بالرفع

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: In the familiar reading, lā negates the genus, denying the very reality of doubt and therefore every individual instance; the nominative reading likewise contradicts the affirmation of even one doubt.
rows.anchor: إن قوله : { لا ريب } نفي لماهية الريب ونفي الماهية يقتضي نفي كل فرد

rows.speaker: نافع
rows.claim: Nāfiʿ and ʿĀṣim pause after “lā rayb”; that pause requires an understood predicate, as in the idioms “no harm” and “no problem,” common in the Hijaz, yielding “there is no doubt; in it is guidance.”
rows.anchor: وعن نافع وعاصم أنهما وقفا على { لا ريب } ولا بد للواقف من أن ينوي خبرا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The well-known pause after “fīhi” is preferable: it makes the Book itself guidance, whereas the other pause says only that guidance is contained in it; the Qur’an is repeatedly called light and guidance.
rows.anchor: القراءة الأولى أولى ؛ لأن على القراءة الأولى يكون الكتاب نفسه هدى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Rāzī defines guidance as indication (dalāla), rejecting definitions that make it guidance received or knowledge.
rows.anchor: الهدى عبارة عن الدلالة ، وقال صاحب الكشاف : الهدى هو الدلالة الموصلة إلى البغية

rows.speaker: الزمخشري
rows.claim: Al-Zamakhsharī defines guidance as an indication that conveys its recipient to the goal.
rows.anchor: وقال صاحب الكشاف : الهدى هو الدلالة الموصلة إلى البغية

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Guidance need not result in being guided: God says He guided Thamūd, yet they chose blindness, and Arabic permits “I guided him, but he was not guided.”
rows.anchor: أثبت الهدى مع عدم الاهتداء ، ولأنه يصح في لغة العرب أن يقال : هديته فلم يهتد

rows.speaker: الزمخشري
rows.claim: Al-Zamakhsharī argues from the contrast between guidance and error, the praise implied by “guided,” and the fact that iḥtada is the responsive form of hadā, like breaking and being broken, that guidance reaches its goal.
rows.anchor: واحتج صاحب الكشاف بأمور ثلاثة : أولها : وقوع الضلالة في مقابلة الهدى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Rāzī replies that misguidance opposes guidance, while error opposes being guided; only those who benefit are called guided, and an unused means counts as if nonexistent.
rows.anchor: الفرق بين الهدى وبين الاهتداء معلوم بالضرورة ، فمقابل الهدى هو الإضلال ومقابل الاهتداء هو الضلال

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The analogy with “commanded and obeyed” does not establish that guidance entails its recipient’s response; “I guided him, but he was not guided” directly counters that inference.
rows.anchor: أن الائتمار مطاوع الأمر يقال : أمرته فائتمر ، ولم يلزم منه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Guidance cannot mean knowledge alone, because God calls the Qur’an guidance although the Qur’an itself is not knowledge; guidance therefore means indication.
rows.anchor: وصف القرآن بأنه هدى ولا شك أنه في نفسه ليس بعلم ، فدل على أن الهدى هو الدلالة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Taqwā is the active participle of waqā, to protect; protection is intense guarding. Since the verse praises the God-fearing, it especially means observing worship and avoiding prohibitions in religious matters.
rows.anchor: المتقي في اللغة اسم فاعل من قولهم وقاه فاتقى ، والوقاية فرط الصيانة

rows.speaker: بعضهم
rows.claim: Some say taqwā includes avoiding minor sins, just as minor sins are included in threats of punishment.
rows.anchor: فقال بعضهم : يدخل كما يدخل الصغائر في الوعيد

rows.speaker: آخرون
rows.claim: Others say minor sins are not included in taqwā; all agree that repentance for every sin is obligatory, and dispute only whether a person who fails to avoid minor sins still merits the name muttaqī.
rows.anchor: وقال آخرون : لا يدخل ، ولا نزاع في وجوب التوبة عن الكل

rows.speaker: النبي ﷺ
rows.claim: A report from the Prophet says a servant does not reach the rank of the God-fearing until he leaves harmless matters out of caution against harmful ones.
rows.anchor: فروي عنه عليه السلام أنه قال : ( لا يبلغ العبد درجة المتقين حتى يدع ما لا بأس به

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās describes the God-fearing as those who fear punishment for abandoning what desire inclines them toward and hope for mercy by affirming what God sent.
rows.anchor: وعن ابن عباس رضي الله عنهما : أنهم الذين يحذرون من الله العقوبة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Taqwā can mean fear of God, as in commands to fear the Lord, fear Him, and fear the Day of Judgment.
rows.anchor: واعلم أن التقوى هي الخشية ، قال في أول النساء : { تفلحون يأيها الناس اتقوا ربكم }

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Depending on context, taqwā in the Qur’an denotes faith or tawḥīd, repentance, obedience, refraining from sin, or sincerity; the cited verses illustrate each usage.
rows.anchor: والغرض الأصلي منها الإيمان تارة ، والتوبة أخرى ، والطاعة ثالثة ، وترك المعصية رابعا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Taqwā is an exalted station: God is with those who fear Him and do good, and the most honored before God are the most God-fearing.
rows.anchor: إن أكرمكم عند الله أتقاكم

rows.speaker: النبي ﷺ
rows.claim: In a report attributed to the Prophet through Ibn ʿAbbās, the most honored person is the one who fears God, the strongest is the one who trusts God, and the richest is the one more confident in God’s provision than in his own possessions.
rows.anchor: وعن ابن عباس قال عليه السلام : ( من أحب أن يكون أكرم الناس فليتق الله ، ومن أحب أن يكون أقوى الناس فليتوكل على الله

rows.speaker: علي بن أبي طالب
rows.claim: ʿAlī defines taqwā as not persisting in sin and not being deluded by one’s acts of obedience.
rows.anchor: وقال علي بن أبي طالب : التقوى ترك الإصرار عل المعصية

rows.speaker: الحسن
rows.claim: Al-Ḥasan says taqwā is choosing no one over God and knowing that all affairs are in God’s hands.
rows.anchor: قال الحسن : التقوى أن لا تختار عل الله سوى الله ، وتعلم أن الأمور كلها بيد الله

rows.speaker: إبراهيم بن أدهم
rows.claim: Ibrāhīm ibn Adham defines taqwā as having no fault found by people in one’s speech, by angels in one’s deeds, or by the Lord of the Throne in one’s inward self.
rows.anchor: وقال إبراهيم بن أدهم : التقوى أن لا يجد الخلق في لسانك عيبا . ولا الملائكة في أفعالك

rows.speaker: الواقدي
rows.claim: Al-Wāqidī says taqwā is adorning one’s inward self for the Truth as one adorns one’s outward self for people.
rows.anchor: وقال الواقدي : التقوى أن تزين سرك للحق كما زينت ظاهرك للخلق

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Other definitions say the God-fearing do not appear where their Lord has forbidden them, or follow the Prophet, leave worldly life behind, seek sincerity and fidelity, and avoid the unlawful.
rows.anchor: ويقال : التقوى أن لا يراك مولاك حيث نهاك ، ويقال : المتقي من سلك سبيل المصطفى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Since the Qur’an is called guidance for all people in 2:185 and here for the God-fearing, al-Rāzī infers that the God-fearing are all people; one who is not God-fearing is, as it were, not human.
rows.anchor: أنه تعالى بين أن القرآن هدى للناس في قوله : { شهر رمضان الذى أنزل فيه القرآن هدى للناس } ( البقرة : 185 ) ثم قال ههنا في القرآن

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Although the Qur’an is evidence for believers and unbelievers alike about the Creator, religion, and the Messenger’s truth, al-Rāzī names the God-fearing because they are the ones who benefited from it; if guidance means conveying to the goal, it applies only to them.
rows.anchor: القرآن كما أنه هدى للمتقين ودلالة لهم على وجود الصانع ، وعلى دينه وصدق رسوله ، فهو أيضا دلالة للكافرين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: An objection says the Qur’an cannot be guidance when it contains ambiguous passages, depends on reason to distinguish clear from ambiguous, and appears to contain opposing claims about compulsion and free choice.
rows.anchor: كيف وصف القرآن كله بأنه هدى وفيه مجمل ومتشابه كثير ؛ ولولا دلالة العقل لما تميز المحكم عن المتشابه

rows.speaker: علي بن أبي طالب
rows.claim: Al-Rāzī cites ʿAlī’s warning to Ibn ʿAbbās, sent to debate the Khārijites, not to argue from the Qur’an because it admits two interpretations.
rows.anchor: نقل عن علي بن أبي طالب رضي الله عنه أنه قال لابن عباس حين بعثه رسولا إلى الخوارج

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Rāzī replies that ambiguous and concise passages remain guidance because their intended meaning can be identified through reason or transmitted evidence.
rows.anchor: ذلك المتشابه والمجمل لما لم ينفك عما هو المراد على التعيين وهو إما دلالة العقل أو دلالة السمع صار كله هدى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A further objection says the Qur’an cannot guide to knowledge of God, His attributes, or prophecy if its own authority must already be established for it to prove them.
rows.anchor: كل ما يتوقف صحة كون القرآن حجة على صحته لم يكن القرآن هدى فيه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Guidance need only concern some matters, such as defining religious laws or confirming rational knowledge; it need not cover everything. Al-Rāzī says this proves an unqualified expression does not imply universal scope.
rows.anchor: ليس من شرط كونه هدى أن يكون هدى في كل شيء ، بل يكفي فيه أن يكون هدى في بعض الأشياء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Against the claim that a text with many conflicting interpretations cannot be clear guidance, al-Rāzī answers that the criticism applies to exegetes who merely list conflicting views; he has preferred one by evidence.
rows.anchor: من تكلم في التفسير بحيث يورد الأقوال المتعارضة ، ولا يرجح واحدا منها على الباقي يتوجه عليه هو هذا السؤال

rows.speaker: الزمخشري
rows.claim: Al-Zamakhsharī allows “guidance for the God-fearing” to be nominative as a predicate of an omitted subject, conjoined with “no doubt,” or a subject predicated by the preceding adverb; it may also be an accusative circumstantial phrase.
rows.anchor: الرفع ؛ لأنه خبر مبتدأ محذوف

rows.speaker: الزمخشري
rows.claim: Al-Zamakhsharī sees four independent, unjoined statements—alif-lām-mīm, “that Book,” “no doubt in it,” and “guidance for the God-fearing”—as a tightly interlinked sequence.
rows.anchor: إن قوله : { الضالين الم } جملة برأسها ، أو طائفة من حروف المعجم مستقلة بنفسها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Rāzī favors the sequence’s rhetorical force: the opening signals the challenge, the Book is declared supremely perfect, doubt is denied as testimony to that perfection, and guidance confirms its certainty.
rows.anchor: نبه أولا على أنه الكلام المتحدي به ، ثم أشير إليه بأنه الكتاب المنعوت بغاية الكمال

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The four clauses gain force respectively through ellipsis and delicate allusion, the grandeur of definiteness, placing “doubt” before “in it,” and ellipsis plus the indefinite verbal noun “guidance” instead of the adjective “guiding.”
rows.anchor: ففي الأولى الحذف والرمز إلى الغرض بألطف وجه ، وفي الثانية ما في التعريف من الفخامة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: General wording may be specified, including by rational proof: 2:284 would otherwise imply that God has power over Himself, which reason rules out.
rows.anchor: لأن قوله : { والله على كل شيء قدير } ( البقرة : 284 ) يقتضي أن يكون قادرا على نفسه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The objection that a general word shown not to include every item makes the Qur’an false is answered by noting that kull commonly denotes a majority figuratively as well as the whole collective.
rows.anchor: لفظ الكل كما أنه يستعمل في المجموع . فقد يستعمل مجازا في الأكثر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Rāzī introduces the following verses as an argument establishing divine unity, prophethood, and resurrection.
rows.anchor: القول في إقامة الدلالة على التوحيد والنبوة والمعاد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: After describing believers, unbelievers, and hypocrites, God shifts from speaking about them to addressing them directly, an iltifāt also seen in 1:5.
rows.anchor: أقبل عليهم بالخطاب ، وهو من باب الالتفات المذكور في قوله تعالى : { إياك نعبد وإياك نستعين }

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Direct address stirs and moves the hearer more than continuing to speak about that person in the third person.
rows.anchor: أن فيه مزيد هز وتحريك من السامع

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The shift honors and draws the addressee near: after initially making the Messenger an intermediary, God now addresses the person without an intermediary.
rows.anchor: كأنه سبحانه وتعالى يقول . جعلت الرسول واسطة بيني وبينك أولا ثم الآن أزيد في إكرامك وتقريبك

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The move from third to direct address suggests that a servant engaged in worship is continually ascending.
rows.anchor: أنه مشعر بأن العبد إذا كان مشتغلا بالعبودية فإنه يكون أبدا في الترقي

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Because the earlier verses narrated their condition and these verses impose difficult commands, God’s direct personal address gives relief and makes the burden pleasant.
rows.anchor: الآيات المتقدمة كانت في حكاية أحوالهم ، وأما هذه الآيات فإنها أمر وتكليف ، ففيه كلفة ومشقة فلا بد من راحة

rows.speaker: علقمة والحسن
rows.claim: ʿAlqama and al-Ḥasan say that Qur’anic addresses “O people” are Meccan, while “O you who believe” is Medinan.
rows.anchor: حكي عن علقمة والحسن أنه قال : كل شيء في القرآن

rows.speaker: القاضي
rows.claim: Al-Qāḍī accepts that distinction if it rests on transmitted reports, but rejects deriving it merely from the larger number of believers in Medina: believers may be addressed as people, and unbelievers may be commanded to worship just as believers are told to persist and increase in worship.
rows.anchor: هذا الذي ذكروه إن كان الرجوع فيه إلى النقل فمسلم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Words normally denote linguistic or nonlinguistic things; the vocative particle is different, functioning as an act that draws attention rather than denoting another thing.
rows.anchor: لفظ النداء لم يجعل دليلا على شيء آخر ، بل هو لفظ يجري مجرى عمل يعمله عامل لأجل التنبيه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “O Zayd” cannot mean “I call Zayd”: the latter is a truth-apt report, does not itself make Zayd the addressee, may be spoken to a third party, and reports rather than performs the call.
rows.anchor: أن قولنا . أنادي زيدا ، خبر يحتمل التصديق والتكذيب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Though names are strongest and particles weakest, a name can join a particle in calling; by analogy, a human can serve the transcendent Lord through invocation and humble supplication.
rows.anchor: قد يأتلف الاسم مع الحرف في حال النداء ، فكذا البشر يصلح لخدمة الرب حال النداء والتضرع

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Yā originally calls someone distant; hamza (a-) calls someone near. Using yā for someone nearby treats an inattentive or heedless person as distant.
rows.anchor: ( ياء ) حرف وضع في أصله لنداء البعيد وإن كان لنداء القريب لكن لسبب أمر مهم جدا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Although God is nearer than the jugular vein, a supplicant says “O Lord” either from humility and self-reproach, distancing himself from the stations of intimacy, or because answering prayer is supremely important.
rows.anchor: هو استبعاد لنفسه من مظان الزلفى وما يقربه إلى منازل المقربين هضما لنفسه وإقرارا عليها بالتنقيص

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ay connects the vocative to a noun bearing the definite article, just as dhū and alladhī connect generic nouns to descriptions and definite nouns to clauses; ay is ambiguous and needs a noun or equivalent adjective to specify it.
rows.anchor: ( أي ) وصلة إلى نداء ما فيه الألف اللام كما أن ( ذو ) و ( الذي ) وصلتان إلى الوصف بأسماء الأجناس

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The vocative particle governs ay, while the following noun is its adjective, as in “O Zayd, the courteous”; unlike Zayd, ay cannot stand independently and therefore remains joined to its adjective and described noun.
rows.anchor: فالذي يعمل فيه حرف النداء هو أي والاسم التابع له صفة كقولك يا زيد الظريف

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The inserted attention particle reinforces the call and compensates for the genitive construction expected with ay.
rows.anchor: التنبيه المقحمة بين الصفة وموصوفها ففيها فائدتان

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The emphatic formula is frequent in the Qur’an because its commands, prohibitions, promises, threats, and momentous histories must awaken listeners who are heedless.
rows.anchor: إن كل ما نادى الله تعالى به عباده من الأوامر والنواهي ، والوعد والوعيد ، واقتصاص أخبار المتقدمين بأمور عظام
